item.title: When Words Aren’t What They Seem
item.description:
Cognition

When Words Aren’t What They Seem

How false friends fool the brain.

Posted September 4, 2026

Key points
  • False friends are words that look or sound alike across languages but have different meanings.
  • Our brains use familiar patterns to make sense of new words, and sometimes get it wrong.
  • The same connections that cause confusion can also help us learn a new language.

Learning another language can feel a little like making new friends. Some words are immediately familiar. Others take time to get to know. And then there are the false friends: words that look reassuringly familiar but turn out to mean something quite different.

Linguists use the term false friends, or, in French, faux amis, for words that look or sound similar across languages but differ in meaning. They can be a source of confusion, but they also reveal something interesting about how our minds process language.

Linguistic Look-Alikes

First, the good news is that familiarity really can help. Words sharing a common ancestor are called cognates. English night, French nuit, German Nacht, and Swedish natt, for example, can all be traced back to the same linguistic family. The same goes for English book, Dutch boek, and Norwegian bok. Cognates are like linguistic cousins. Their resemblance in sound, spelling, or meaning gives language learners something to grab onto. The more closely related two languages are, the more of these helpful similarities they are likely to share.

But when learning another language, our brains don’t always know when a shortcut is reliable. Consider French avertissement. It looks just like the English advertisement, but instead it means “warning” or “caution.” An advertisement is une publicité. The resemblance between the two words is therefore tempting, but misleading.

This is where false friends become psychologically interesting. When we encounter something unfamiliar, we don’t process it from scratch. We draw on what we already know, using patterns, context, and previous experience to generate predictions about what a word might mean. This reflects a broader process known as cross-linguistic influence: when people know more than one language, knowledge from one language can affect how they process another.

For bilinguals and language learners, this means that words can activate information from more than one language. Research suggests that when bilinguals encounter a word, their brains can activate related words in both languages, even when they’re only using one (Ryskin, 2023). Predictable words are generally easier and faster to process than unexpected ones. But the same shortcuts can sometimes lead us astray. A familiar-looking word can activate a meaning that turns out to be wrong for the language or context we’re actually using.

When Words Fool Us

False friends can produce some memorable mistakes. Spanish embarazada looks suspiciously like English “embarrassed,” but it means “pregnant.” The Spanish word for embarrassed is avergonzado or avergonzada. These are reminders that a familiar-looking form does not guarantee a familiar meaning.

article continues after advertisement

Many well-known false friends have a decidedly taboo side. The Swedish word bra means “fine” or “well.” So, an English speaker encountering bra in Swedish might momentarily think they've wandered into a conversation about underwear, only to discover that everyone is actually talking about something being good. The two words aren’t related. The Swedish word bra comes from an older word braf, meaning “good” or “brave,” while the English bra is a shortening of the French brassiere.

The Upside of Getting It Wrong

These mistakes are a natural part of learning another language. They show that the learner is actively making connections between their known language and the new one. The problem is that sometimes the connection is stronger than the difference. Research on false cognates suggests that the overlap in word form can actually help learners acquire new vocabulary, even when that same overlap can occasionally lead them astray. (Otwinowska, 2021)

That is one reason false friends are so revealing. They show language learning in action. The brain is constantly comparing, connecting, predicting, and updating. Occasionally, however, the familiar-looking word leads us down the wrong path. Language learning therefore requires more than memorizing vocabulary. It also requires learning when to question our first impression.

After all, in language, as in friendship, familiarity doesn’t always tell the whole story.

item.title: Need help? Need to Disagree? Talk About it in Person
item.description:
Persuasion

Need help? Need to Disagree? Talk About it in Person

Skip the email. The awkward conversation is far more effective.

Posted September 4, 2026

Key points
  • We consistently underestimate the power of in-person conversations.
  • Asking for help in person is significantly more effective than email, phone, or even Zoom.
  • We perceive in-person disagreements as stressful, but are more likely to emerge with mutual understanding.

We’re more persuasive in person than over text, email, or even Zoom. And we can disagree more effectively, getting our point across without stoking conflict, in person. Yet we consistently underestimate the power of in-person interactions over other media.

In-person requests for help are more likely to succeed

In a study by Mahdi Roghanizad and Vanessa Bohns, experimental participants asked their friends for help using various types of media: phone, email, Zoom, and in person.

Participants expected that in-person and Zoom requests would have roughly the same level of effectiveness. Both are face-to-face, real-time methods of communication where you hear the other person’s voice and see their expressions and gestures.

In reality, while the participants’ predictions about their in-person requests for help were more or less accurate, their Zoom requests for help were much less effective than they expected. Their friends were nearly 40% more likely to help when asked in person.

As you might expect, email had the worst results. An earlier study by the same researchers found that requests made in person were 34 times more effective than email. It’s much easier to dash off a quick “no” than to say it in person. The surprising part isn’t that email is so much less effective. It’s that participants in both studies drastically underestimated how much difference it would make to ask in person, versus using any other medium. In-person communication makes a significant difference.

In-person disagreement leads to more understanding and less perceived conflict

A different study by Burint Bevis, Juliana Schroeder, and Michael Yeomans examined spoken disagreement versus written disagreement. In this study, participants exchanged opinions on controversial topics. Initially, most participants preferred the idea of disagreeing in writing. They predicted that written disagreement would produce less conflict and greater understanding, while a spoken conversation would be stressful, contentious, and unlikely to change minds.

The results of the study showed the opposite. When speaking, participants tended to be more receptive to what the other person had to say. Even though they continued to disagree, they were more likely to come to an understanding of each other’s positions and have a more positive experience with the conversation. In contrast, written communication resulted in greater perceptions of conflict and lower levels of understanding.

This result, too, should not be surprising. We’ve all seen how a political Facebook post by a relative can make us breathe fire, while a conversation with the same person on the same topic is likely to be calmer and more respectful. What’s surprising is that we continue to believe that spoken disagreements will be too uncomfortable to endure, while written disagreements will allow people to calmly take in the facts.

article continues after advertisement

In-person conversations make a big difference

Talking to each other – ideally in the same physical space, but if not, using media that allow us to see and hear each other – makes a difference. It makes a difference in how likely we are to help each other, and in how willing we are to accept disagreement and listen to opposing views. Instead of shying away from a tough conversation, and opting for an email or text instead, consider engaging with the person. When we share our humanity, tough conversations can become easier.

item.title: When You Love Them, Do You Like Who You Become?
item.description:
Relationships

When You Love Them, Do You Like Who You Become?

Some relationships expand your identity; others make you disappear.

Posted September 4, 2026

Key points
  • Different relationships can activate different patterns of thought, emotion, and behavior within us.
  • A familiar person may unintentionally pull us back into a role we have already outgrown.
  • Close partners can support or inhibit our movement toward the person we hope to become.
  • Noticing who we become around someone provides valuable information about the relationship.

We like the idea that our self is stable and consistent, something that feels reliable. In reality, different parts of us emerge depending on who we are with.

One of my therapy clients described this fluctuation: "There are people around whom I become funnier. Others make me quieter. Around some people, I find myself apologizing before I have done anything wrong. Around others, I speak with a confidence I didn’t know I have."

For years he believed that his personality belonged entirely to him. Through our work together, he began noticing that different people seemed to summon entirely different versions of himself.

Think of the person around whom you feel most like yourself. Now think of someone around whom you become smaller, more careful, or less recognizable. Perhaps one of the most important questions we can ask about a relationship is not simply, "Do I love this person?" It is, "Who do I become when I am with them?"

influence
Source: Gerlat / Pixabay

We do not carry one fixed personality that's unchanged from room to room. Different relationships awaken different memories, expectations, defenses, and possibilities within us. Research on the relational self suggests that our mental representations of significant people can activate corresponding patterns in how we experience and express ourselves (Andersen & Chen, 2002).

Others’ expectations can shape our sense of self and our behavior. People who have known us for a long time may unintentionally continue relating to us as our old self. In their presence, we can find ourselves returning to an old role long after we have outgrown it.

This leads to a more challenging insight about relationships: We can love someone deeply and still dislike the person we repeatedly become around them. Evaluating a relationship may require us to look not only at how we feel about the other person, but also at how they shape our own way of being.

In psychology, we call it the Michelangelo phenomenon: Close relationships “sculpt” us toward—or away from—our ideal self. Research found that when a close partner’s perceptions and behavior affirm our ideal self, we are more likely to move toward that version of ourselves (Drigotas et al., 1999). People who recognize and support the person you hope to become can make that version of you easier to find and express.

article continues after advertisement

This is not about blaming other people for the versions of ourselves that emerge around them. Relationships are co-created, shaped by both people’s histories, expectations, fears, and patterns. Still, the person we repeatedly become in a relationship is important information.

Every relationship is a room with its own emotional climate. In some rooms we stretch out and breathe deeply; in others we instinctively make ourselves smaller.

We may not choose every relationship in our lives, but we can become more conscious within each one. Sometimes, simply noticing who we become is the first step toward choosing a different way of being.

Which relationships allow more of you to exist?

item.title: Your Breakdown May Actually Be Your Promotion
item.description:
Identity

Your Breakdown May Actually Be Your Promotion

What feels like life falling apart may be an invitation to become someone new.

Posted September 4, 2026

Key points
  • A breakdown can signal that an old identity no longer fits who you’re becoming.
  • Growth often begins when you stop trying to rebuild the life you’ve outgrown.
  • Self-trust means trusting yourself to meet what comes next, even without certainty.
  • The breakdown isn’t the promotion. Who you become through it can be.

There are seasons in life when it feels like everything starts falling apart at once. Your relationship changes, the business slows down, money gets tight, your health demands your attention, or something you counted on disappears. Maybe nothing dramatic happens at all, yet the life that once excited you suddenly feels like it doesn’t fit anymore.

Our first instinct is usually to ask, “What did I do wrong?” Yet what if that’s the wrong question? What if some breakdowns are actually evidence that the version of you who created your current life has reached the edge of what it can create?

I want to be careful here because I don’t want to lead with every painful experience “happens for a reason.” Trauma and loss are real, and terrible things happen that don’t need to be wrapped in a motivational quote and called a blessing. And psychology also shows us that human beings have a remarkable capacity to grow through adversity.

Researchers Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun call this "post-traumatic growth," which can include greater personal strength, deeper relationships, changed priorities, and a greater appreciation for life (Tedeschi & Calhoun, 2004). In other words, the breakdown itself isn’t the promotion. It’s who you can become through it.

Source: pixabay / pexels

We’re Wired to Protect the Familiar

Human beings like predictability. Even when our current circumstances aren’t ideal, there's comfort in knowing who we are, how our world works, and what tomorrow will probably look like. This is why transformation can feel threatening.

You can consciously want a bigger business, healthier relationship, fitter body, deeper sense of purpose, or a completely different life while another subconscious part of you is protesting, “Absolutely not. It may not be my dream life, but I know how to survive here.”

Uncertainty can be deeply uncomfortable, especially when our sense of identity gets disrupted. Research on self-concept clarity suggests that having a clear and coherent sense of who we are is associated with psychological well-being, while disruption to that sense of self can increase distress and our difficulty tolerating uncertainty (Sharratt et al., 2020).

So we cling to the familiar by overthinking, controlling, procrastinating, self-sabotaging, and recreating old patterns. Sometimes we run back toward the very thing we said we wanted to leave because at least we know who we are there, even if it feels like we are trapped in purgatory.

I see this all the time with high performers and have personally previously felt trapped in this purgatory, too. They interpret discomfort as evidence that something has gone wrong, when sometimes discomfort simply means the old map no longer matches the territory.

article continues after advertisement

When Your Identity Has Expired

One of the most powerful questions I ask people is, “Who are you without the identity that got you here?”

I’ve had to answer that question myself many times through different identities as a water polo player, bodybuilder, celebrity trainer, nutritionist, business owner, founder, medicine man, author, and coach. Every one of those identities has been real, and every one served a purpose and helped create a chapter of my life.

An identity can become a prison when we confuse who we have been with who we are allowed to become. We start protecting the costume instead of listening to the person wearing it.

This is one reason major life disruptions can shake us so deeply. We aren’t only losing the relationship, job, business, role, status, or circumstance. Sometimes we’re losing the person we believed ourselves to be inside of it. Research on identity disruption suggests that adversity can affect self-concept clarity, essentially destabilizing our sense of who we are (Vartanian et al., 2018).

That can be incredibly painful… and it can also create an opening.

Stop Trying to Get Your Old Life Back

When life changes unexpectedly, our instinct is usually restoration. How do I get my business back to where it was, get that relationship back, find my motivation again, get my old body back, or become the person I used to be?

However, there’s another question I find far more powerful:

“Who is this experience asking me to become?”

That question changes the orientation completely. Instead of desperately trying to recreate yesterday, you become curious about tomorrow.

This connects directly to what I call "total self-trust. Self-trust means trusting your ability to meet whatever comes next rather than believing everything will work out exactly the way you want it to work out. There’s a huge difference: One requires controlling life, while the other requires learning to trust yourself inside of life.

article continues after advertisement

Research on resilience has found that people demonstrate multiple pathways of adaptation following loss and potentially traumatic experiences. In fact, resilience may be far more common than we once assumed (Bonanno, 2004). Sometimes strength is recognizing that you don’t belong where you used to be anymore.

The Hallway Between Identities

Transformation has an uncomfortable middle. I call it the chrysalis, like the stage between a caterpillar and a butterfly. The old version of you isn’t working anymore, while the next version hasn’t fully arrived. I think of it like standing in a hallway after one door has closed while the next one hasn’t opened yet.

Most people hate the hallway because there’s no applause, no certainty, and no clean five-step plan. Your old strategies may stop producing the same results, yet you don’t know what will replace them.

Admittedly, this stage sucks. And it’s where people often panic and run backward. They return to the relationship, recreate the old business model, overwork, overtrain, overspend, fill the silence, or chase another achievement, anything to feel like themselves again.

Remember, the hallway may be exactly where the deeper work is happening. When familiar sources of identity and validation disappear, you have the opportunity to discover something much more durable, being who you are without them.

Post-traumatic growth research suggests that highly challenging experiences can force people to reconsider assumptions about themselves and their lives. That struggle can sometimes lead to new priorities, greater personal strength, and a fundamentally different life narrative (Tedeschi & Calhoun, 2004).

article continues after advertisement

The keyword is "sometimes." Growth isn’t guaranteed by suffering; it comes from what we do with it by integrating the lessons.

Don’t Waste the Breakdown

When something significant falls apart, there is a natural desire to fix it as quickly as possible. Before you do, get curious. Ask yourself: What is this revealing that I couldn’t see before? What am I being asked to release? What have I been pretending still works? Which identity am I desperately protecting? Where have I been outsourcing my sense of safety, worth, or direction? What would I choose next if I deeply trusted myself?

These are uncomfortable yet powerful questions, because a breakdown has a way of stripping away noise. Underneath that noise, you may discover that you knew something needed to change long before circumstances forced the conversation.

Maybe your body knew, your enthusiasm disappeared, or you kept getting that quiet feeling that something wasn’t right, but your mind kept negotiating.

Expand Into Who You’re Becoming

In my E.M.P.O.W.E.R. Process, this connects to Expand. Expansion is widening your capacity to hold uncertainty without immediately running back to what’s familiar, learning to say, “I don’t know exactly what comes next and I trust myself enough to find out.” That’s a very different kind of confidence.

Life often contracts before it expands. Businesses expand and contract, relationships change, bodies change, careers evolve, identities shift, and life moves through seasons. We create unnecessary suffering when we assume every contraction means we’re moving backward, when sometimes contraction creates the space required for the next expansion.

The Bottom Line

Rather than being punished or demoted, maybe you’re being invited to stop rebuilding something you’ve already outgrown. The promotion is who you have the opportunity to become because you chose to meet it differently.

So if life feels uncertain right now, resist the urge to immediately label this season a failure. You might simply be standing in the hallway, where the old door has closed and the new one isn’t open yet.

article continues after advertisement

Stay curious, and instead of only asking, “Why is this happening to me?” try asking, “Who am I becoming through this?"

item.title: Dolly: A Childfree Inspiration for Us All
item.description:
Altruism

Dolly: A Childfree Inspiration for Us All

How those without children shape philanthropy and community.

Posted September 4, 2026

Key points
  • Dolly Parton didn't have kids, but she supported early childhood literacy.
  • The childless and childfree give more of their estates to charity than parents do.
  • Lack of networks hinders large-scale philanthropic collaboration among childfree donors.
Source: Matt Benson/Unsplash

Endowed as she was with the voice of an angel and a physicality she so adroitly applied for comedic purposes, Dolly Parton’s legacy will never be silenced. Dolly was not criticized for not having children. Instead, she’s heralded as a beacon of balance, generosity, and good humor.

With no children of her own, Dolly’s Imagination Library benefits over three million youth aged five and younger around the world. Each month they receive books at no cost, planting seeds for future literacy and love of reading. “The seeds of dreams are often found in books,” she said, “and the seeds you help plant in your community can grow across the world.”

Giving is often without show, and efforts are often woven into our very character. Like Dolly, many of us who are without children equivocate when grilled about why we don't have children. Part of the reason we don’t often tell our stories is that most involve the complexity and evolution included in living outside the mainstream of parenthood. Being non-parents is an element of our being, not a statement of our value.

Our crucial role in philanthropy and giving cannot be understated, though. Whether supporting lives on our family tree or giving to charities, many childless and childfree people contribute our time and treasures to support those in need. We make a mark that is not insignificant.

For example, those of us without children are much more likely to include a charity in our estate plans than parents. According to a study by Russell James, Professor of Charitable Financial Planning at Texas Tech from 1992 to 2012, 50 percent of childless decedents left money to philanthropic organizations versus 17.1 percent of those with children.

As childless and childfree adults, what we lack is a way to combine our giving to create lasting change. I’ve long thought if such a mechanism existed, together we could band together to balance disparities in intergenerational transfer of wealth, combat climate change, or nourish the hungry. But routes for unification of our demographic are few.

Before COVID-19, I was involved in planning my local community foundation’s event for women donors who don’t have kids. The event was packed, and participants clamored for future events tailored to our interests. Although the organization agreed, years later, another event has yet to come to fruition. No one can tell me why.

article continues after advertisement
Source: Josh Applegate/Unsplash

I can guarantee, though, that as a result of that first event, several new donor advised funds were established, and numerous liaisons and friendships were instigated. I have a small donor advised fund that will, upon my demise, support early childhood literacy.

After I cut back on my professional work life, I donated years of service to the primary grades, supporting children who struggled with reading and writing. Recalling the choruses of their greetings each time I entered the classroom nourishes me to this day; so do the drawings they put in a memory book when I moved away.

Those of us who are still star-struck may fail to see the the power of Dolly’s role in making the world a better place, not only for children but also by serving as a model for how we can better get along with one another. She offers inspiration for how to be thriving members of our communities who don’t happen to have kids. What more could one want as their life’s legacy?

item.title: Lessons on Healing 25 Years after 9/11
item.description:
Grief

Lessons on Healing 25 Years after 9/11

Healing from loss is often a journey best made with companionship.

Posted September 4, 2026

Key points
  • Loss and subsequent grief reactions are universal human experiences.
  • The earliest of records provides us with the insight that the process of grief is a journey best shared.
  • Peer support is a uniquely powerful means of assisting those beset by the angst of grief navigate the journey.

Contributing authors:

Cherie Castellano, CSW is Vice President for Survivor Services at TAPS and was a member of the New York Emergency Services 9/11 Delegation to England and Ireland

Lisa Zucker, MSW is Senior Director of Education at TAPS

Bonnie Carroll is the Founder and President of the Tragedy Assistance Program for Survivors (TAPS) and recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Barack Obama in 2015

George S. Everly, Jr., PhD, MA is on the faculty of The Johns Hopkins School of Medicine and served on the NYPD and Columbia University initiatives at Ground Zero post 9/11

Source: wikiimages/ Pixabay

The pain of loss surely extends to time immemorial. It is safe to say that the experience of grief is a universal human experience extending far prior to written records. Societal and religious traditions of lamentation are legion. The earliest written records in Western civilization are replete with mentions of grief. Evidence from the Old Kingdom of Egypt (2600 BC) suggests the mourning of a loss was a public experience involving great pomp and circumstance, especially in the case of the wealthy and ruling class. The 5th-century Greek tragedies were large‑scale public rituals for the cathartic expression of loss and trauma. The tragedies made grieving a civic experience, if not an obligation. The Nordic and Germanic traditions continued the theme of grief as a civic responsibility, but in these cases, grief was expressed in public mythological storytelling and ritualized remembrances such as funerals. With the rise of Christianity and other religions, organized public funerals spread in popularity. Grief was one of the centerpieces of the birth of psychology in the late 1800s and early 1900s. Freud’s Mourning and Melancholia (1917) marked the first formal psychological theory of grief, emphasizing the importance of “letting go” of that which was lost.

But more recently, Freud’s notion of letting go has been challenged. Reformulating the connection in a different manner (reattachment) with that which was lost is favored more than the detachment advocated by Freud (Klass, Silverman, & Nickman, 1996). So, we see the process of grieving loss has been characterized by public displays and rituals throughout history. Grieving has been understood as a process that is best shared rather than denied or hidden away. If there was one relatively recent watershed moment that concretized the notion of never forgetting, it may well be the events of September 11th, 2001.

article continues after advertisement

An Approach to Large-Scale Healing

As we approach the 25th anniversary of September 11th, we reflect on the thousands of lives lost that day, the thousands more affected by illness, and the families forever changed by the subsequent wars and military service. For example, the Tragedy Assistance Program for Survivors (TAPS) has provided support for over 100,000 bereaved family members since its inception, with 14,858 9/11-related bereaved military family members served since 9/11/2001. In order to fulfill such a mission, the approach of providing psychological support through the exclusive use of licensed mental health clinicians had to be abandoned. Peer support models were adopted instead.

The Peers

Peers may be defined as two or more people who share some common denominator, typically shared lived experiences. Individuals who have successfully navigated challenging life experiences can, with proper training, effectively serve in a peer support capacity. These peer supporters can harness the bond of shared experience to create credibility, perceived empathy, and hopefulness (SAMHSA, 2015). Peer support is recognized and endorsed by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Administration (SAMHSA). In the wake of September 11, 2001, peers were trained and mobilized to provide support to military families, but in order to harness the power of peer support, those peer supporters were those who had experienced the pain of similar losses, but had healed.

In the TAPS approach, peers were trained in a simple three-step non-linear bereavement model:

  1. Provide safety and stabilization: Offering immediate crisis intervention and acute support when grief is first activated. Creating a psychologically safe space is essential.
  2. Foster a healthy grief journey: Providing supportive care, peer support, and therapy, as indicated, while individuals process strong emotions and memories.
  3. Assist with making meaning: Helping individuals find purpose, honor their loved ones, and build meaningful lives moving forward.
article continues after advertisement

Lesson Learned

Decades of walking alongside bereaved families confirms that peer support can be profoundly therapeutic. These same principles are now being applied in the Ukraine. So, as we find ourselves looking back, we see a three-fold revelation: 1) grief is a process best seen as a journey, 2) the journey is best undertaken with companionship, and 3) the best companions are those who have made a similar journey before. There is healing in being able to sit with someone who does not need grief explained, who understands that there is no timetable for mourning, and who can offer living proof that it is possible to survive devastating loss while continuing to carry love forward.

Twenty-five years after 9/11, and in the case of TAPS, a core promise remains unchanged: no one who is grieving the death of someone who served our nation should ever have to walk that road alone. Survivors caring for survivors has been at the heart of helping from the beginning, and it remains one of the most powerful expressions of healing, hope, and the enduring bonds of love. This promise can be made to all survivors of loss regardless of its origin. So, it seems the ancients got it right. They understood that healing from loss should never be a solitary experience. The support of others, especially peers, teaches the essential lessons of love and hope.

item.title: The Mysterious Mushroom That Makes You Gulliver's Companion
item.description:
Hallucination

The Mysterious Mushroom That Makes You Gulliver's Companion

Seeing is believing, until everyone sees the same impossible thing.

Posted September 4, 2026

Key points
  • Lanmaoa asiatica lacks psilocybin and ibotenic acid, yet it causes a hallucination of fantasy tiny people.
  • Lilliputian hallucinations appear across cultures and centuries with consistent, relatively similar features.
  • Brains construct perception through prediction, not pure sensory data, per neuroscience research.
  • Shared hallucinations challenge our assumption that collective experiences constitute verifiable reality.

For most people, the world around them appears certain and obvious beyond any doubt. We have sensory receptors that perceive information from the external world. However, the brain's perception of reality is not as simple as we think. The objects and events we face daily, even though they appear very real to us, might not be real at all. This time, not only philosophers but also neuroscientists are in consensus on this complexity. Modern neuroscience suggests that the brain uses sensory signals to make predictions about external information that favor our survival rather than fitting with reality. We can give many examples of errors in visual, auditory, and other sensory systems.

Lisa Feldman Barrett provides a compelling example at the opening of her book, Seven and a Half Lessons About the Brain. She says that a soldier in the civil wars of southern Africa, while doing drills in the forest, suddenly spots what appears to be a line of camouflaged fighters armed with AK-47s. His heart pounding, he raises his rifle and flips off the safety, until a comrade grabs his arm and says, "Don't shoot, it's just a boy." He looks again and sees a ten-year-old herding cows with a stick, not a rifle. The writer tells this story to show how predictive processing works: The soldier's brain had built a strong prior perception from past combat experience and imposed it on ambiguous sensory input, nearly overriding what was actually there. It has been suggested that the brain uses sensory input just to correct these predictions [1].

The perception of reality is even more complicated than we suppose

Perhaps many people, like me, have become familiar with a mysterious Chinese mushroom, Lanmaoa asiatica, recently studied by researchers at the University of Utah. Researchers investigated two kinds of mushrooms by sequencing DNA samples from Yunnan, China, and the Philippines. They found that both mushrooms are the same species, despite having different names in the two regions. They also confirmed that these mushrooms do not contain any known hallucinogenic compounds, such as ibotenic acid or psilocybin. However, people in southwestern China and the Philippines knew hundreds of years ago that consuming this mushroom raw or semi-cooked causes them to see tiny people jumping, climbing, and running around them. The condition is named “Lilliputian hallucination” [2].

Hallucinogenic mushrooms are not unusual, as seen in Amanita and magic mushrooms. Additionally, other compounds, such as psychedelics, can produce profound hallucinations. Common hallucinogenic substances, such as psilocybin, produce hallucinations that differ from person to person depending on their mindset, culture, and experience. They include mostly color-shifting patterns, warped geometry, and changing visual textures. However, this particular mushroom induces a completely different effect.

article continues after advertisement

Lilliputian hallucination is also seen with other mental disorders

The name of this condition, Lilliputian hallucination, was first coined by the French psychiatrist Raoul Leroy in 1909, inspired by Jonathan Swift's tiny islanders in Gulliver's Travels. It has been observed during alcohol withdrawal, in certain stages of dementia, Alice in Wonderland syndrome, schizophrenia, and even in macular degeneration, where the eye itself is failing rather than the mind. Leroy himself personally experienced these visions and noticed the same pattern in his patients. The main characteristic of this condition is a relatively consistent experience: seeing fantastically small humans within a real environmental background, occurring across a wide range of conditions.

Is the shared illusion a reality?

Some neuroscientists argue that everything we call perception is really an inference, the brain's best guess built from fragments of sensory signal about what's out there. Anil Seth, a neuroscientist at the University of Sussex, calls this a "controlled hallucination": What we experience as a solid, stable world is a prediction the brain generates and only occasionally corrects with the senses, rather than a direct readout of reality [3]. If that's true, then the line between a hallucination and ordinary perception isn't as sharp as we'd like to think—both are constructions, and the only real difference is how tightly one is anchored to incoming sensory data. So how do we ever get close to the "real" at all? Perhaps the answer isn't philosophical but statistical: When enough people construct the same illusion, independently, without communicating with one another, we stop calling it a hallucination and start calling it the truth.

Chinese mushroom revolutionizes our perception of reality

A mushroom that produces a shared hallucination — shared not in the sense of two people perceiving the same scene together in the same room, but in the sense that unrelated individuals, across cultures, eras, and continents, arrive at the identical vision independently — apart from its biological appeal and the nature of its psychoactive compound, raises important philosophical questions. First, why is it that most people who consume this mushroom raw, or who experience Lilliputian hallucinations for other reasons, see small people a few centimeters tall? Why don't they see, for instance, aliens? Do all these afflicted people carry some prior belief about little people, or does the brain inherently contain this fantasy? Are there regions in the brain where the elements of hallucination, dream, and imagination reside, and does our mysterious chemical compound use this reservoir of memory to produce hallucinations? And most importantly of all, does this mushroom teach us that even when a perception is the same among a population of people, we should still doubt whether it is real?

Previously, strange claims by individuals about witnessing supernatural phenomena were easily attributed to hallucination. Now, we must also doubt collective experiences of strange events. If a hallucination can be shared independently by so many people, the line between "subjective error" and "objective reality" becomes blurrier than we ever imagined. Someone once said, half-jokingly, that maybe these little people are real, and under ordinary conditions we simply do not see them, but this mysterious mushroom opens our eyes to them.
